_comment: The phone script: everything the suspects say when you call them, in one place.
Edit this file to rewrite any conversation - it is read at runtime, so nothing needs rebuilding.
Each suspect is matched to the scene by 'name' (their display name, e.g. 'The Mayor', or their
prefab name, e.g. 'Mayor'). Any field left blank here falls back to what the suspect was authored
with on the Interrogation Room Director in MainScene.
basic          line 1 - what they say when they pick up, before any clue is put to them
nonsense       line 2 - their answer to a clue that means nothing to them
correct        line 3 - the moment the one true clue lands and they know they are caught
explanation    line 4 - them explaining themselves, one array entry per paragraph (can be long)
correctClueKey the clue that breaks them: a notebook clue key (see the director's 'List Clue
Keys' context menu) or another suspect's specialClueId
specialClueId  the id this suspect's special clue is unlocked under, so another suspect's
correctClueKey can point at it and the calls chain together
specialClue    the text of that special clue, read on the phone and written in the notebook
stages         a confrontation that takes more than one clue, walked in the order written. Each
step has a clueKey it wants, a 'waiting' line asking for it without naming it, and
a 'response' read a paragraph at a time once it lands. A suspect with stages
ignores correct, explanation and correctClueKey - it is all in the steps.
The detective (the player character) is not on the phone, so there is no entry for them here.
The case runs as three strands of two calls each. The player opens each strand with one of the
three answers in Resources/CorrectClues.json:
cuts on his hands -> Pianist  -> knifeFight    -> Chief -> knifeInGarage   (the weapon)
the ring          -> Widow    -> ringFromMayor -> Mayor -> ringWasDiamonds (the reason)
the grape order   -> Henchman -> theNote       (the appointment)
All three ends meet on the Baron, who is confronted in steps: the note, then the knife, then the
ring. He concedes each one and asks for the next without saying what it is, so the case cannot be
closed until every strand has been walked.

suspects.name: The Baron
suspects.basic: Baron speaking. Make it quick, detective.
suspects.nonsense: That means nothing to me, detective, and I have people waiting.

response: ...she kept it. Nine years of picking up after me and she kept it.
Very well. I wrote to him. I write fifty notes in a day, detective, and I am not going to stand here pretending my own hand is a forgery.
But look at what you are holding. That note says I wanted a word with a member of my staff. It does not say I got one.

stages.waiting: You are still on the line, so I take it you believe you have more than my handwriting. A note is not a body, detective. If you mean to tell me how a man died in my garage, start with what did it.
response: A knife. On a shelf. In a garage, which is where a household keeps its tools.
Half that party walked past that shelf on the way to their cars, and one of them was your own chief of police, who put it there himself and has said nothing about it since.
So you have a weapon that anybody at all could have lifted. You still cannot put it in my hand.

stages.waiting: A note, and a knife half the county could have held. What you do not have is a reason. I had never spoken to the man in my life. Tell me why someone in my position would trouble himself with a waiter, and then you and I can discuss what became of him.
response: ...he swore to me that ring went in the river. He looked me in the face and told me it was gone.
Diamond would not sell. I made him three offers and he laughed at the third one, so I stopped making offers.
I paid a man to make it look like a burglary. He did it well enough that your own chief of police spent two years telling a widow she had done it herself.
I never paid him the rest of what was owed. Why would I? Where was he going to take that complaint? He kept the ring instead and told himself that made us even.

Then he turned up at my own birthday party carrying a tray, and poured a full glass of wine down my front so he could stand close enough to say a number in my ear. At my table, in my house, with the mayor sitting four feet away.

So yes. I wrote him a note, and I went out to the garage to settle it. He put his hands on me. There was a knife on that shelf that was not mine and had no business being there at all, and the whole thing took less time than it takes to tell you about it.
I paid him in the end, detective. Just not in money.

suspects.name: The Chief
suspects.basic: Chief here. This had better be important.
suspects.nonsense: That is not a question, that is a guess. Come back when you have something.
suspects.correct: ...how could you possibly know that? He told you. The piano player told you.
explanation: Fine. I had the knife. I have said all along that I had no weapon on me, and that was a lie, and standing here now I would tell it again.

The piano player got mouthy about the way I was talking to Mrs Diamond. I had a knife off the waiter's tray in my hand before I knew I had picked it up, and he took hold of the blade. There was blood on the floor and the mayor was forty feet away.

I could not walk back into that room holding it, and I could not put it back on the tray with his blood on it. So I went out to the garage and left it on the shelf over the workbench, and I came back inside and stood there and said nothing.
Thirty one years I have done this job. I left a knife lying where anyone at that party could pick it up. Somebody did.
suspects.specialClue: The Chief left the carving knife on the shelf over the workbench in the garage, and there it stayed, in reach of anyone who went out to the cars.

suspects.name: The Henchman
suspects.nonsense: I have nothing to say about that.
suspects.correct: ...how could you possibly know that? I have not been able to eat a grape since I was nine years old.
explanation: The plate was not for me. Anyone who has worked a night with me knows what grapes do to me. I say it out loud at every job so that nobody kills me by accident.

The baron told me before midnight that he would be outside and that I was to bring him grapes when I had a minute. It was gone one before I got the plate made up, and gone two before the room let go of me long enough to carry it out to him.
He was on the floor of the garage. Leo. I hired him for that party, I hired both of those boys myself, and he was lying there by the workbench.
There was a note on the floor by his hand. Meet me at the garage at 12 AM, and the baron's name under it in his own writing, the way he signs everything.
I put it in my pocket. Nine years of picking things up after that man, and my hand did it before my head could stop it. I have it still, detective, and I am tired of having it.
suspects.specialClue: A note found on the garage floor beside the body, in the Baron's own hand and signed by him - meet me at the garage at 12 AM. Amara Steel kept it.

suspects.name: The Mayor
suspects.basic: You have reached the Mayor's office. Speak.
suspects.nonsense: No comment, and I would remind you who you are speaking to.
suspects.correct: ...she told you. Of course she told you. I did ask her to keep it between the two of us.
explanation: All right. Yes. I bought it, and I bought it standing in a garage, and I am not proud of the setting.

I had gone out to the car because that waiter cut me off and I keep a bottle in the glovebox. The other one was out there, the young one, and he had a ring in his hand and he wanted cash for it that night.
I knew that ring, detective. I have sat across a table from that ring at three separate dinners. It was Diamond's.

And I bought it anyway, because I had spent the entire evening trying to think of something to give Amelia that no other man in that room would have thought of, and there it was in front of me. I did not ask him where he got it. I did not want an answer I would have had to do something about.
So I put it in her hand and went back to my party feeling like the cleverest man alive. You may write that down.
suspects.specialClue: The Mayor bought the ring off Leo Silvers in the garage that night, and knew it for Mr Diamond's - which puts Leo in the Diamond house the night Diamond died.

suspects.name: The Pianist
suspects.basic: Hello? I was in the middle of practising.
suspects.nonsense: I do not know anything about that. I only play the piano.
suspects.correct: ...how could you possibly know that? I have not been able to play a scale in a week.
explanation: My hands. I did not catch them on anything. I put them round a blade.
That policeman had been at Mrs Diamond all evening, telling half the city she killed her husband. Somebody had to say something to him about it, so I did, out by the service door where the trays go.

He did not care to be spoken to that way. He took the carving knife off the waiter's tray and held it out at me, and I grabbed it. That is what these are. Anyone who has ever taken hold of a blade by the wrong end has them.
Then he walked off with it, and I went back to my piano and sat on my hands for the rest of the night. No, I did not report it. Report it to whom, detective? He is the man you report things to.
suspects.correctClueKey: hadAt|The Pianist|cuts on his hands|1 AM
suspects.specialClue: The Chief took the carving knife off the waiter's tray during a scuffle with the Pianist and walked away with it, an hour before the murder.

suspects.name: The Widow
suspects.basic: Yes? Who is calling at this hour?
suspects.nonsense: I do not see what that has to do with me.
suspects.correct: ...how could you possibly know that? I have not taken it off. I have not been able to look at it either.
explanation: The mayor gave it to me. He came in from outside somewhere before midnight, very pleased with himself, and put it in my hand and closed my fingers over it as though he had invented kindness.
It is my husband's ring. It was on his hand the day he died and it was gone by the time they let me see him. They told me it was a burglary, they closed the case, and they told me to be grateful.

So a man hands it back to me at a birthday party, while the chief of police is going round that same room telling everyone I murdered my husband for his money. What was I to do, detective? Stand up and announce it?
I put my hand in my lap and I said nothing. And while I sat there saying nothing, a waiter was dying sixty feet away.
suspects.specialClue: The ring the Widow was wearing is her late husband's, missing since the night he died, and the Mayor put it into her hand before 1 AM.
